item.title: There's No Such Thing as a Free Video Game
item.description:
Adolescence

There's No Such Thing as a Free Video Game

Why "free to play" games often cause the most harm.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Many video games can be downloaded for free.
  • Free-to-play video games typically use more psychological tricks to keep people playing and spending money.
  • Because of these tricks, free-to-play video games often have the most negative impact on players.

Every video game has a cost. Before letting your kids download a game, make sure it only costs money.

As a therapist, I work with a lot of teenage gamers and their parents. One of the first questions parents ask me is whether the games their children are playing are harmful. “He plays a lot of Minecraft. Is that one okay for kids?”

I spend a lot of time thinking about video games, playing them, reading about them, and talking to gamers. I even wrote a book explaining video games to parents. But with millions of games available to download, I haven’t always heard of the games in question. Many games are harmless fun, but some are habit-forming, wallet-depleting machines. Luckily, there’s an easy shorthand to find out which type it is.

My first three follow-up questions to parents are usually, “What kind of game is it?” “Is it single-player or multiplayer?” and “Was it free to download?” That last question is perhaps the most important. To understand why, we need a little bit of a history lesson.

When video games first started to become popular in the 1980s, arcades charged 25 cents per play. If the games were too easy, a talented gamer could tie up a machine for a long time after paying just one quarter. This meant that games like Pac-Man, Space Invaders, and Galaga were tuned to suck quarters out of a gamer’s pocket as efficiently as possible. They were hard, sometimes frustratingly so, because every time the player lost, they would need to spend more money on the game to keep going.

Eventually, home consoles like the NES and Sega Genesis allowed consumers to buy a full game up front and play as much as they liked. Game designers no longer needed to focus on getting as many quarters as possible and could focus on creating a fun experience that consumers would pay for.

In the late 1990s and early 2000s, some game developers started to experiment with a free-to-play (F2P) model. In this model, anyone could download the game for free, with the option to buy microtransactions—optional purchases including extra equipment, characters, or bonus features. Surprisingly, offering the product for free turned out to be by far the most profitable. The top F2P games now reliably make tens or hundreds of times more money than even the most popular paid games.

They accomplish this by employing every psychological trick they can. For example, most free games include “inconvenient gameplay elements" such as adding artificial timers to the game. Want to upgrade your castle’s turrets to better ward off invaders? Your virtual workers will be done in eight real-life hours. In the meantime, your castle will be vulnerable. Unless you pay us one dollar.

Or you might have a magical shield around your castle that lasts for twelve hours. Don’t worry though, it recharges whenever you open the game. You only have to open the game twice a day to protect your hard-earned resources from other players. Or give us five dollars to keep the shield active all weekend.

article continues after advertisement

And for the next week, we’ll have a special event with exciting new quests to complete, powerful new weapons, and fun new ways to customize your character. But the event will only last seven days, so you’d better play a few times a day to make sure you don’t miss out. You can also access the higher-tier, super-exclusive, this-week-only content for just $20. If you fail to play enough this week, don’t worry, you can buy all of the new content for just fifty dollars (a one hundred dollar value!).

Candy Crush's in-game shop offering purchases up to $99.99
Source: Candy Crush Saga

For vulnerable players, such as gambling addicts, children, or those who simply struggle with self-control, this can become a serious problem. According to a recent survey, almost one-in-five Japanese people in their twenties have spent so much money on in-game purchases that they struggled to cover living expenses.

In short, many games have started to return to the original model of nickel-and-diming their player base. But in the 40 years since the halcyon days of Pac-Man, they’ve developed enough tricks to keep gamers hooked and, for some, create a clinical addiction.

I’ve worked with a lot of gaming addicts over the years, and in almost every case, it was centered around a free-to-play game. Roblox, League of Legends, Candy Crush Saga, Fortnite, Clash of Clans, Destiny 2, Pokémon GO…are all free-to-play. If you’re a parent and you’re considering whether a game could become a problem, look for how it’s monetized. I believe that it’s worth paying for a game to ensure that the game developers won’t try to manipulate your child into spending more time or money on a game than they can afford. They don’t need to, they already have your money.

Unfortunately, this strategy isn’t bulletproof. Popular games like Call of Duty, EA Sports FC, and GTA Online have successfully had their cake and eaten it too. Even though players pay full price up front, they still ask for more, using all of the F2P tricks at their disposal to make their games addictive.

article continues after advertisement

A more effective strategy is to look for whether the game has microtransactions. If they do, be wary. This information is easily found by Googling the name of the game plus “microtransactions” or on websites like Common Sense Media. In Common Sense Media’s writeup of NBA 2K25, for example, they note under “Products and Purchases” that “NBA 2K25 allows for in-game purchases, or microtransactions, which can give players an edge over those who don't make purchases.”

Wherever there are microtransactions, there are game design choices that make problems more likely. Even people who never spend a cent on a game often end up paying for it–through time and missed opportunities. I regularly talk with teens who spend their school lunch hour (or classes) on their phones making sure they take full advantage of an in-game event. I’ve worked with a number of adults who dropped out of college after failing to balance the expectations of a free game with schoolwork.

Many of these problems would have been reduced or eliminated if they had chosen a paid game instead. In short, when your kids ask permission to download a new game, check to see how much it costs and whether it has microtransactions. Be very, very careful if it’s free. It might cost something more valuable than money.

Andrew is the author of Parenting a Gamer: Help Your Child Build Healthy Habits, Make Positive Choices, and Find Balance in Virtual Worlds.

item.title: AI Hysteria: Is the Sky Really Falling?
item.description:
Emotional Contagion

AI Hysteria: Is the Sky Really Falling?

Why AI alarmism echoes past tech scares.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • There is a long history of exaggerated fears around threats posed by new technologies: AI is just the latest.
  • The threat once reserved only for the A-Bomb has been redirected to existential-risk narratives about AI.
  • Concerns that AI will escape safeguards and wreak havoc on humanity, are the stuff of science fiction.

Recently, fears have emerged over the dangers posed by AI. While we should exercise caution regarding health and safety concerns around new technologies, such fears are nothing new and have all the hallmarks of a moral panic: an exaggerated or unfounded fear over a perceived threat that poses a grave danger to society. These panics are frequently accompanied by rumors, scaremongering, and sensational media reports that stoke public anxieties.

A Short History of Tech Fears

Soon after the invention of the telephone, switchboard operators began reporting a new condition dubbed “Telephone Sickness” that was supposedly caused by the crackling sounds that were a common feature of the early phone system. Workers attributed these sounds to an array of health complaints, from nausea, headaches, and dizziness to concussion-like symptoms. By 1899, a writer in the British Medical Journal warned that talking on the phone could trigger “excitability,” “giddiness,” and nerve damage. Such fears grew out of mass suggestion which reflected popular anxieties of the time.

When personal refrigerators began to gain widespread use in the 1920s, they often contained small compartments for making ice cubes. Yet in the early years of refrigeration, many people were afraid to drink beverages with these cubes, believing that mechanically produced ice was unnatural and could make people sick. The popular alternative was far more dubious: ice chipped from blocks that had been extracted from frozen lakes, rivers, and streams.

When AM radio emerged in the early 20th century, some people complained that the invisible waves were causing illness. There were even fears that it was disrupting weather patterns. There were similar fears around the advent of television. In the early years of TV, some psychologists warned that children would become passive zombies, unable to think for themselves, with parents told it would cause everything from poor eyesight to moral decay. By the late 1960s, there were concerns that color television sets were emitting hazardous levels of radiation, eventually prompting congressional investigations. While a small number of defective sets were found to emit high levels of radiation, subsequent studies revealed that the danger had been greatly exaggerated.

Predictions that AI will hollow out entire professions overnight are also nothing new. When the sewing machine came into widespread use in the 19th century, it sparked concerns that the jobs of tailors and seamstresses would soon be obsolete. Similar worries coincided with the invention of the typewriter, as it was believed that scribes and clerks would be left unemployed. Ironically, the use of typewriters generated more office jobs than it destroyed.

article continues after advertisement

In the early 20th century, when farming relied heavily on the use of horses, oxen, and farmhands, there were widespread fears that the invention of the tractor would cause large-scale unemployment. Politicians and newspaper editors warned of the threat that tractors posed to the American way of life. The reality was cheaper food and higher productivity, with many farm workers taking up new opportunities created by these technologies in construction, factories, healthcare, education, and in the retail sector. More recently, during the 1970s, teachers and mathematicians raised the alarm over students being given access to calculators, believing they would cripple their ability to think mathematically.

Fears around the threat of new technologies have been a major theme throughout history. More recently, there have been unfounded health scares around the use of mobile phones, Wi-Fi, and 5G towers, with people believing that exposure to these new technologies is responsible for everything from brain tumors and childhood cancers to memory problems and neurodegenerative disorders.

The AI Scare: Old Wine in New Skins

What is striking is how predictable this cycle is. Job-loss fears once aimed at calculators and sewing machines have resurfaced as warnings that AI will replace entire professions overnight. The biological dread once projected onto radio waves and television sets has reappeared as concern in the press that chatbots are inducing “AI psychosis,” even though the evidence for AI directly causing psychotic illness is thin. Hence, many psychiatrists prefer the term “AI-associated delusions” because AI is simply providing the content and feedback loop for the delusion.

None of this means every concern about AI is unfounded. There are legitimate questions about labor markets, misinformation, and safety testing that deserve serious engagement. But the shape of the fear, its speed, its intensity, its tendency to outrun the evidence, is exactly the shape every transformative technology has produced before it. We have seen this story many times. Only the technology changes.

Amid the gloom and doom surrounding artificial intelligence, we would do well to remember one important fact: while AI was created by humans, it is not human. The AI scare tells us more about us than it does about it. For AI reflects age-old human anxieties. It’s not the first technology scare, and it won’t be the last.
